## Answer Key: Chapter 1 {#sec-solutions-ch1}

Full solutions to Chapter 1's "Check your understanding" questions
(@sec-ch1).

**1. Quick check. What does the residual stream carry from one block to the
next?**

*Answer.* The running sum of the original embedding plus every
sublayer update added so far -- not just the most recent sublayer's raw
output. Per the residual update $x^{(l+1)} = x^{(l)} + f(\text{Norm}(x^{(l)}))$,
each block *adds* its sublayer's output onto the existing stream value;
it never replaces the stream with just the new sublayer's output.

*Common trap:* "the output of the most recent attention or MLP
sublayer" -- that describes only the update being added in that step,
not the accumulated stream value.

**2. Explain. Why does a decoder-only objective allow one-token-
at-a-time generation?**

*Answer.* Because the causal mask restricts every position to
attending only to itself and earlier positions, the same forward-pass
structure used in training also directly defines how to generate: at
each position, produce a next-token distribution conditioned only on
what came before. A bidirectional encoder's positions can attend to
*later* positions too, so its representation at a given position
already depends on tokens that would not exist yet during generation --
that structure cannot be reused one token at a time the way a causal
one can.

*Common trap:* "decoder-only models are just smaller/simpler" -- size
is unrelated; the difference is specifically about which positions are
allowed to attend to which.

**3. Calculation. $d_{\text{model}} = 8$, $H_q = 2$, $S = 5$: find
$d_{\text{head}}$ and the shape of $QK^\top$ for one head.**

*Answer.* $d_{\text{head}} = d_{\text{model}} / H_q = 8 / 2 = 4$. The
raw attention score matrix for one head is $(S, S) = (5, 5)$ -- one
score per query/key pair, regardless of $d_{\text{head}}$.

*Common trap:* $(S, d_{\text{head}}) = (5, 4)$ -- this confuses the
per-head attention *output* shape (which is $(S, d_{\text{head}})$)
with the score matrix shape (always $(S, S)$).

**4. Misconception check. "Causal masking means each token can
only attend to the immediately previous token."**

*Answer.* False. Causal masking allows a position to attend to *every*
position at or before it ($j \le i$), not only the single immediately
preceding position. The mask is $0$ (allowed) for every $j \le i$ and
$-\infty$ (blocked) only for $j > i$ -- a full lower-triangular region,
not a single diagonal band.

*Why:* conflating causal masking with a fixed local window
(sliding-window attention, a separate mechanism covered in a later
chapter). Causal masking alone imposes no limit on how far back a
position can look.

**5. Misconception check. "The residual stream is a separate
memory database the model writes facts into and reads back later."**

*Answer.* False. The residual stream is a single vector per position,
updated additively in place -- not a separate, queryable store. Every
sublayer's output is added directly onto the same fixed-width vector
that already exists at that position; there is no separate storage
structure and no mechanism for a later block to selectively "query"
what an earlier block specifically wrote. It can only read the
accumulated sum.

*Why:* taking this chapter's own receipt analogy too literally -- a
real receipt's lines stay individually readable; the residual stream's
contributions are summed into one vector and cannot be individually
read back out. This is exactly the analogy's stated breakdown point.

**6. Design exercise (applied exercise). Full tensor-shape trace for your own
toy config.**

*Answer.* For config $(d_{\text{model}}, L, H_q)$ with $d_{\text{model}}$
divisible by $H_q$: input vector $(d_{\text{model}},)$; $Q$/$K$/$V$
before splitting, $(d_{\text{model}},)$ each (or $(S, d_{\text{model}})$
for a full sequence); after splitting into heads, $(H_q, d_{\text{head}})$
where $d_{\text{head}} = d_{\text{model}} / H_q$; per-head attention
output, $(d_{\text{head}},)$ per head; concatenated across heads, back
to $(d_{\text{model}},)$; final vector added to the residual stream,
$(d_{\text{model}},)$ -- matching the input shape exactly, since
addition requires matching shapes.

*Common trap:* forgetting to concatenate the per-head outputs back to
$d_{\text{model}}$ width before the output projection and residual
addition -- leaving the answer at the per-head shape.

**7. Interview practice. "Walk me through what happens
differently between processing a 500-token prompt versus generating
the 501st token."**

*Answer.* A strong answer: (1) names prefill -- conceptually, all 500
positions evaluated together, building per-layer K/V state for every
position (a serving engine may chunk this for scheduling reasons
without changing the logical picture); (2) names the decode step --
exactly one new position processed, computing only its own new K/V and
reusing the 500 cached K/V rows unchanged; (3) explicitly states that
generating the 501st token does not reprocess or re-read the first 500
tokens.

*Interview criteria:* does the answer name both phases correctly, does
it state what specifically is reused (K/V rows) versus recomputed (the
one new position's K/V), and does it avoid the "re-reads the whole
prompt" framing this chapter's headline misconception warns against?

*Common trap:* "decoding is faster because the prompt is already
processed," without stating what specifically is reused or why that
reuse is what makes it faster.
